blocks.x: I was wondering if you ever made any records?
Alfred Williams again, I'm back on. No. Never made any records?
I already made some in California about 1921. I guess you left right before. I was gone. I think Fred Washington was on that.
Do you remember Fred Washington? Yeah, I left. Did you know I'm down here? Fred Washington, yeah. He used to play at E. Lala's, E. Lala's Nightclub, yeah. He played with a band or a solo?
No, he was a band. They had a band.
Just like we making up nice. Yeah. He was just a make up band, like good fellas, you know.
Who were some of the other piano players around town?
Well, Steve Lewis and Tony Jackson. You knew him? No, I didn't know him. I knew of him. I didn't know him.
Did you know this guy Alfred Wilson?
Wilson?
No, I didn't know him. I knew of him. He was a piano player here. I just thought you'd know him because of the names or something, you know. I imagine you've heard of him. No, I didn't know him.
Alfred Carroll? No, I know Alibrad Alexander.
David Medipiro's band.

Oh, I was a man. You know Udell Wilson. Oh, Udell, yes, indeed. Who wouldn't know Udell? Yes, indeed. Yeah, Udell. And this other piano player, I'm trying to think of his name, he went to Chicago, never come back. New York, at least.
Do you remember Frank Ahamia? Frank Ahamia, no, I don't remember that.
It's all my time. What's Campbell's name?
Arthur Campbell. Arthur Campbell.

Arthur Campbell. Arthur Campbell. Arthur Campbell. I heard of him. Steve Lewis used to talk about him all the time. Yeah. Monnie, do you remember? Oh, Monnie Jones, yeah. Monnie, yeah. Cripple fellow. Yeah, I know Monnie. That's Buddy Christian.
What's your name?
Buddy Christian, I know him. Clarence Williams. Yeah. I know all them old timers. Who did they work with, Buddy Christian? Buddy Christian played down at Pete Lowndes, too.
He was at Pete Lowndes at one time, you know.

Yeah, he was at Pete Lowndes at one time, you know. Yeah, he was at Pete Lowndes. Yeah, he was at Pete Lowndes, too. Did you ever work with Buddy Petitia? Oh, yeah. I worked with Buddy Petitia about two years. When was that? That must have been around, no, it couldn't have been two years. I worked with Buddy Petitia. In 21, when I came back from Los Angeles in 1921. Must have been about eight months, then I joined Sam Morgan's band, you see. Of course, I worked with Sam from 21 to 25, you see. Who was in Buddy's band?
I don't remember. I've been writing just now.

What kind of tunes did they play? Well, they called it that time Ragtime, you know. Ragtime, then they changed the name to jazz. They brought the same kind of a beat as far as the new bands of present girls. Oh, yeah.
Oh, the same band.
Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah.
Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah.
Oh, yeah.
Oh, the same thing.

Yeah, the same beat. And they played more than Scott Joplin numbers, you know. See, they played a lot of them. But he wasn't a reading musician, you know. Yeah. Just a routine, as we call it, trumpet player, you know. But he was good, very good. I can't think of who he had in this band. I know he had Simon Marrera at one time playing with him.
He had a lot of different people. He had Zeb and Fred Monroe.
Oh, yeah. Zeb. Yeah, that's right. He had a bunch, you know. See. Pills with him on the line. Yeah, yeah. Buddy Man of Day was with him. Oh, yeah. George Washington.
The trombone.
That's right. Little George Washington. He had a thing. He changed him so fast. Because Buddy was, wasn't reliable, you know.
He's been a little. Were you in the band before Faiso or after Faiso?
Must've been after Faiso. Must've been after Faiso. Faiso left here way early twenties. What become of him? I don't know.
I don't know where he is. Never did hear either. No. I think I haven't thought to ask anybody really what's happening. No, no.
I ask a lot of people when I come back. They say they didn't have heard from him. Last time they heard, I believe it was around in Texas somewhere. Galveston or San Antone or somewhere.
Well, you would've seen him in San Antone maybe.
No, no. I'm 600 miles from San Antone. Where were you? You were in El Paso.
What years were you there? How long were you there?
I was in El Paso from 36 to 51. From 36 to 51.
All through the war and then the last one. That's right.
I was on that job, that picture that you see on the band. I stayed on that job.
You have any New Orleans guys out there with you? No.

I had one guy. He came out in 46, Bob Watts. What did he play? Trumpet. Most of the time I had a mixed band. Some of the time I had white Mexicans. On the last I had, nobody was in the band. But me, I had four Mexicans with myself for about three years until my job closed.
What kind of music did the Mexicans play? My kind of music. College music. American music. They were, man. They were, man.

They could play American music. American music. American music. Fine musicians. Yeah, fine musicians. Yeah, they played American music. Would they play New Orleans style jazz? No, they couldn't. They couldn't. They tried.
But they did the best they could. All right.
Oh yeah. We made them like it. Oh yeah. We made them like it. Because I learned them. You see, because I learned them a lot about our tunes.
They had very good ears. They knew the music.
And the ears was very good.
And the ears was very good.
And they would come. And after little Bob Watts come out there.
Well, they learned a lot of the tunes.

Because he could play them. You see. He learned a lot of our tunes. Oh yeah. They learned a lot of them. He had a fine tenor man and a clarinet guy. He was very good. I took them off to a head. Very fine. What kind of dancing did they do over there? Any jitterbugs? Oh yeah. Them young people. That's right. I don't know if there was any sort of western kind or Mexican style. Or anything else. Or anything else. I did. I did. I did.
I did.
I did.
I did. I did. I did. I did. I did. I did. I did. I did. I did. I did.

No, well we had to play all that music. You had to play that different music. You got to play Spanish music. The white people even like it. Yeah, the natives, you know. You got to play Mexican music, you got to play hillbilly, and you got to play American jazz. You got to play them all. Right now I tell these guys, I say, man, you're all right, you're playing, you're playing all right, but they got some Mexican music. Guys have never played. They were so surprised, you know, that I caught on to it, you know. He said, just to show you what experience to do. See, I was an experienced drummer, you see. And I told them, I said, now don't be afraid now, because I'm the manager of the band. They tell me, because I don't know, I never played Spanish music, you know, I'm asking music. They was a little shy, you know, about me being a manager, you know. I told them, I said, don't be shy, I want to learn. And I learned and they were just tickling to death. I mean, I didn't read, I couldn't read, you know. See, they just would have a voice with me, you know, see. Yeah. And I mean, I'd catch right on and they'd get all the Mexican musicians out of Juarez to come over and hear their drummer. And they were surprised by me, you know, you see. And he said, boy, he can't read.
He said, no, he can't read.

Well, how do you get all them licks and them beats and that music? Some of it was real hard, you know. Yeah. Yeah, it was real hard. He said, we taught it. And I mean, man, I knocked it out. I like it. I really like it. It's nice and it's beautiful. It's beautiful. It's nice music, yes indeed. And them trumpet players, oh man. Beautiful tone. What? Tones. Awesome. Yes indeed. We had a young trumpet player. We had a Mexican show, a flow show about four girls. And that Mexican boy played that hard music and I mean, not a piece of music in front of him. I don't see how the world he can do it. Well, they told me just like the American musicians, just like we play our music without any music, it's the same thing. Yeah. But his music was so complicated, you know.
I was surprised and a youngster.

But a lick of head, oh Lord. It was a lick of head but very fine. His disposition was alright. I liked him. I really liked that kid. Yes indeed. But you have to play Mexican music. Yes indeed. Anytime you get out there in the Middle West. After you leave San Antone. Hillbillies and everything.
We left something out.

After you left Perez, who did you play with? After I left Manny Perez. You mean the orchestra when I was playing on the roof garden? Mm-hmm. I told you I went down to La Vida. You went to La Vida. And then? Got with Ridgely. You with... With Bebe Ridgely's Tuxedo. That band split up at the time. Yeah, see that band split up at the time.
The Celestan's part of them or something? That's right, that's right. And how long were you with Ridgely?

I was Ridgely about a year. See, 28. Then I went to La Vida in 29. There you see. Stayed in La Vida's, 29. 30. 31. 32. I went to Piran. I went to Piran from 32 to 35. Went up on the boat with Piran. Made a trip with Piran in 34 on the JS.
Did you go all the way up to St. Paul or how far?
No, we went to Red Wing. JS turned around.
Almost as far, yeah. That's right.
They say it was close.
Yeah, they say it was close.
Steamer Capital went up there. See, and the JS went for his Red Wings.
Did you stay in St. Louis quite a while?
No, just a day. Just a day. Just a day. See, we went up to Ohio and to Mississippi.
Yeah.
We was a tramp steamer. Yeah, I know. Yeah, see.
I used to go there when I was a boy.

I hear that. Nah. See, we were a tramp steamer, but the steamer capital went to St. Paul and stayed all the summer. See, but not to JS. Yeah. See, she just was a tramp steamer. We'd go up to Ohio first as far as Wheeling, West Virginia. And then we'd come back down to Cairo. Then go up to Mississippi, to Red Wing, Minnesota. Played Muscatine. All them towns up there. Mississippi River. Wisconsin. Also. I really enjoyed it. It was a nice season. I really enjoyed it.
What was P. Ron like then? I mean, his band broke up before.
No, well, I don't know. I wasn't here. I left in 36. He still had his band intact. Everybody but me. I don't know what happened.
No, I mean, in 32 or so.

Oh, he broke up with P. the book out there. Yeah. He just quit the band. See, he quit the band with P. the book out there. Then he made up this band. See, he consists of me, Eddie Pearson, Leo Desjard, Joe Phillips, Arthur Durbney, Elliot Taylor, Manuel Sayles, and Simon Moreira. And a singer by the name of Harold Wells. That was his band. And we played together from 32 until 35. I did.
And I left the band in 35.

And went back to the La Vida. And stayed there a while, about five or six months. And in 36, February the 15th, 1936, I left here with the Georgia Ministry from the Palace Theater. That's right. I stayed with them from February the 15th until March the 25th. They stranded us in El Paso, Texas. That's right. That's where I got stranded, El Paso, Texas. It made it good for me. Yes. Stayed right now. Right there. Stayed there 16 years.
That's right.
Made it good for me. Played all that Southwest. Arizona, New Mexico, Texas.
Who was the manager of that Georgia Minstrel? Do you remember anything else about the company? Who else was in the band?

Well, I didn't know nobody in the band but Kimberl Dial. He the one gave me the job because he played with us on the boat after Elliot Taylor taking sick. They sent to St. Louis and got him and the guys, Simon, taking sick too. Simon Moreira taking sick on the boat. And they sent to St. Louis and got Kimberl Dial and Jimmy Johnson, bass and alto. So Kimberl was the only guy that I knew on the show. Yeah. I didn't know none of the musicians. I didn't know. Just got quaming with him afterwards, you know.
They weren't New Orleans guys?

No. None of them. Different places. Nothing but showmen. That's all they ever played. Show. How fast were you playing that show music? Oh, we had a regular, you see, it wasn't, he had a mental before that, all men. But when he got here, he took a course line, you see. So we played just like a regular nightclub. Yeah, you see. You know. Of course, the grand finale was fast, you know, when you're going off this last show, last of the show, you know. Grand finale, you see. I'll say final, you know. But outside of that, it was all right. Just like you play. One nightclub, blind.
How'd you left here on? You went to La Vida. Who was there in La Vida?
No, we had, we had Ernest Kelly there. Like we had before, Ernest Kelly. Lewis Gibbons. Handley. Raymond Brown. He's living in Frisco. Y'all didn't see Raymond?
No, we didn't see him.
Didn't see him. I didn't see him either. I talked to him, but I didn't see him. I didn't see him.
No, I don't remember. Didn't hear him. Didn't see him. What happened?
I heard his numbers, house and everything, but he didn't come over to see me. I talked to him.
Yeah.
Sydney Flewger, like I said before, to La Vida.
Same band.
Same band.
You were with Sam Morgan, Shabotia, don't you? Yeah.
Yeah, yeah, from 21 to 25.
Did he have any changes in every band?
No, we had about two changes from old band Buddy Manaday to Guy A. Butler Rap.
Excuse me, reinterrupt me, did Sam use a slapstick back in those days? They tell me he used to use a slapstick.

Not much as originally. Baby originally the one. That's the one, yeah, he originated with a slapstick. Top of Sam Morgan, you said that. Well Sam took the pattern after him. Yeah, took the pattern after him. When I was with Sam in them four years, he was...
Oh, he was tops. Four years. He only got about 10 seconds left there.
Sam Morgan was tops, had a fine band.
Well who's the other change? Buddy Manaday went out and who else? But, uh, Simon. And who took his place? T-Boy.
You'll know, you'll know.
...your name and I didn't realize that's where you were born and all that.
What is your name? Let's get it. Alfred Williams.
Any middle name or...?
No middle name.
Let's get us a date on here while we're at it. What's the date?
The date, my, the date I was born? Well today's date is... Today? The date is the 30th. 30th, yeah.
1916. We're recording this at your home, huh? This is where you live? That's right. That's right.
What's the number here? 418 North Prayer.
418 North Prayer. My name's Dick Allen. What's yours?
And then Bill Russell is here and over in the corner, Ralph Allen. Okay, good. You might tell where you were born, Mr. Williams.
I was born in New Orleans, right here. What part of town? In the Third Ward, on Liberty between Lafayette and Padres. 1900 September 1st.
So, uh, can you remember, uh, anything about the, uh, other musicians in the family? Did your mother, father, anybody play against them? Nobody in my family were musicians.
Were you the only child, your brother?
Only child. Only child. Can you remember the first music you heard over in there? Any of the dance bands or parade?
The first music I heard, uh, to remember by being a kid, you know, was the old Tenome Parades.
Oh, yeah.
See, you used to have the old Tenome Parades.
That's right. They had one here.

That's right. Oh, they had more then. Yeah, it was on a Monday. See, the parade was on a Monday and the picnic was that night at the fairgrounds. And the first bands I heard was the old Onward Band, the Excelsior Band, and Papa Celestan's Tuxedo Band, which at that time it was Ridgely's Tuxedo Band. Oh, yeah. Bebe Ridgely's Tuxedo Band.
Bebe Ridgely's Tuxedo Band.
Bebe Ridgely's Tuxedo Band. I used to follow the parades, the street parades, and my famous drummer, Henry Martin, at that time.
He was your favorite.
That was my favorite drummer. He was left-handed. That's why I guess I take him to him, because I was left-handed. Uh-huh. And he taught me and showed me.
How old were you when you started out?
When I started playing, when I played my first job, I was 16. I played with the Columbia Band up on Oak and Protection Levy at a place, a dance hall called Butcher Hill.
Oh, yeah. Johnny St. Sarah told me all the time.
Butcher Hill. Well, I played there with Columbia Band, Tick Chambers. I played in a fella's place. The drummer was with Tick Chambers by the name of Nene.
Right.

That's all I know, Nene. And I played there. We had, in the band at that time, we had Tick Chambers, Ernest Kelly. Ernest Johnson, a little fella they call Duck Ernest, I guess you heard of him. Mm-hmm. And Emmett, the guy who played guitar by the name of Emmett. I don't know, I can't think of his last name, Emmett. And a fella by the name of Roy Palmer, trombone. Oh, yeah, you played with Roy.
I know him in Chicago, yeah. Roy Palmer.
Roy Palmer, he was playing trombone. He was still up there.
I saw him last summer. Living. Yeah, he looks good. I don't know about that. Works in a steel mill, still works hard.
Now, what do you know about that? He does. Yes, indeed. That was my first band I played with. Now, my next band I played with was sitting in a guy's place was with Ori's band.
Well, before we get into that, what I meant to say when you started out, I meant how old were you when you first started?
Sixteen.
With drums or the pick-up drums to learn it.

Oh, the pick-up drums to learn it? Well, I must have been about eight. Eight. About eight years old. I used to play on the front steps, take my mother's dishpan and pots and play on those. Yeah. On her safe, old safe then, what they call a cabinet, kitchen cabinet, not old safe. I used to play on them, play on the front steps. And that's all I liked, all my life, was drums. I didn't care about the other toys and games that the children played.
Did you try to play any other instrument? Never.
That was my instrument. I was a lover of drums. All my life, I wanted to play drums.
Can you remember your first drum set that you got, what it was like, or real drums? No, no, no.

It was, I was playing about two or three years before I was able to get a set of drums. I used to rent my drum from a man called Dave Puykins. Oh, sure. You heard of Professor Dave Puykins. I used to rent my drum from him for a dollar and a half a week.
Did you take any lessons when you were a kid? No lessons. No lessons. No lessons. You, of course, were always left-handed then, so you just picked it up naturally that way? Just, just natural.
Just pick it up naturally. That's right. Never had a lesson. Just like it was a gift. Yeah. Oh, yeah. It was a gift. Mm-hmm.
And you were going to tell about when you joined Kidore.

Yeah, I played in his drummer's place, in Henry Martin's place. Henry Martin was playing out at a place on the, at West End, they call it the Bungalow. I guess you heard of that nightclub, the Bungalow. Well, on Sunday nights, Saturdays and Sundays, that was his busy night out there. He couldn't get off, you see. So after we heard me play with Tick Chambers, well, he said, well, let's try. When it's Kelly, he boosts me up, you know, so I was going to make a good drummer and give him a try. I said, he's a good kid. I said, give him a try. So now my first job I played with, with Kidore and his band was a place they called the Palm Garden. That was on Rampart then, with Rampart all the way up instead of Danilo. Yeah. Between six and seven.
Way up there.

Yeah, way up there. A fellow used to run the place by the name of Vicki Adams. And he had danced there every Sunday night. And I played there with Ori on several occasions. Then after that, that was about in the year.
Who else was in the band with Ori at that time, can you remember?

With Ori at that time, we had Kid Ori, had Mutt Carrier, you heard of Mutt? And Mutt Carrier, trumpet, Johnny Dots, a clarinet, Emile Big Eye on violin, they used violin then, see. Lorenzo Stahls on guitar, you heard of him. Lorenzo Stahls and Eddie Gardner. Oh, on bass. Yes, that was his band. Yeah, that was his band.
Lorenzo Stahls and Eddie Gardner. How many years is that before you went to California that you first played with Ori, do you know?
That must have been about, about two years before I went to Los Angeles.
Who were you working with then? Before you went with him?
Before I went to Los Angeles, I think I was playing with, I think I was playing with, Buddy Petit, when I went to Los Angeles. I went to Los Angeles the year of 1919.

I remember Fass tells about going out there, that he helped organize the group here to go out. That's right. And I know he said he picked up some of the fellows were working out there at Walter Dacu's, maybe at the bungalow out near the lake. Must have been. You weren't in that band though, Walter and Mutt and Wade Whaley, you weren't working with them. No, that's who went with us, Wade Whaley.
Yes.
You weren't working with them at that time?
No, no, no, not at that time. What's happened to Wade Whaley, anyhow? I don't know, I can't hear of him. I don't know what become of him.
We tried to find him out there with Fass that year, we couldn't, no luck at all. That's right. Or he didn't know, or he didn't know at all. That's right, nobody, everybody asked, he didn't know.
Oh, his brother, we'll have to ask him, Bill. His brother? Yeah. That's in the quarter. His brother?
Yeah.
He wants every few years.
I didn't even know he had a brother. Well, I never met him. No, I didn't even know he had a brother.
Can you tell anything about some of the other early drummers that you liked? You mentioned Henry Martin, did you remember any other drummers of that time? Henry Zeno. How did he play? Fine.
Who was he with? He resembled me. See, he was a fellow just on my order. He was playing with Ridgely's Tuxedo Band. Oh, he was really good. At that time. He was a drummer.
With Ridgely's Tuxedo Band.

At that time, Ernest Rapania, he was another drummer. But, you know, he, I didn't like his orchestra drumming, but he was a fine bass drummer in brass bands. And he played with Ridgely's brass band. Oh, yeah. The Tuxedo Brass Band. He played with Tuxedo Brass Band and also Henry Zeno played with orchestra and the brass band at one time, see. And, uh, well, I didn't, you know, look, care about any other drummers outside. Henry Martin was not, he was not a real drummer. I liked him. I liked him. But, uh, Baby Dots, he played with Ridgely a while. He was with the Tuxedo Band a while. He played with Ridgely. That was in the teens. Yeah. See, yeah, that was in the teens, see, around seventeen, eighteen.
But you began working about nineteen sixteen when you were sixteen, you say? That's my first job. I played with a teacher.

That's right, Columbia Band. Mm-hmm. And then after I left the Columbia Band, King Oliver got with Ori, see, just before Storyville closed, you see. And they were working at Pete Lyle's. You heard of Pete Lyle's? Yeah. Well, they were working there. Well, on Sunday night, Saturday and Sundays, King Oliver would go to play with Ori, see, and he would take his drummer. Let me see who was playing at Pete Lyle's then. I can't remember what drummer was playing at Pete Lyle's. But anyhow, Louis Armstrong played in his place. And I played in the drummer's place. And they had a fella named Morris French, you heard of him, trombone player. And we had Steve Lewis on piano. And old man Valto on, you heard of him, on violin. And we played in their place on Saturday and Sunday. That was in the year of nineteen seventeen, just before they closed Storyville. And another guy named Prevo, I guess you heard of him, or clarinet, or Prevo. Louis Prevo. That's a woman. Must have been.
Yeah, I've heard of him.
You heard of him. I don't know what become of him. I don't know what become of him. Quiet kind of fella. Quiet kind of fella, yeah. I don't know what become of Prevo.
Do you remember Red Happy was supposed to be with Oliver sometime? Red Happy. Did you know?
Was he and I do? Red Happy, yeah. Red Happy played with O'Rell Wilde, with King Oliver, I remember Wilde.
What about Ernest Rogers? Was he playing?
Ernest Rogers was playing, but not with known bands, you know. He never was a big with none of the outstanding bands.

Yeah, he never became a singer. That's right, that's right, that's right. He was pretty young in those days, too, I guess. Yes, I guess, you know, Ernest was older than me, I think. In fact, all the fellas were young, we think of them as being older then, because in later years.
That's right, he started playing young. That's right. That's right. That's right.
You mentioned then when you went to California, were there any other bands before you went out there, though, that you can tell us about that you played with?

No, I went out there with O'Rell. I didn't play with nobody but O'Rell. No, I didn't play with nobody but O'Rell. After the band broke up, well they raid the nightclubs, wherever that's so much, you know, and the bands broke up. And I got a job working for the railroad, working cleaning cars for the South Pacific a while. O'Rell, O'Rell, Wade, and Mutt, a guy taking them to Los Angeles, I don't know whether it was Los Angeles or Frisco, a guy that called Curtis Molesby. I guess you heard of him out there. He had nightclubs and everything after that, you know. Well, he take an O'Rell, and Wade Whaley to Frisco while I stayed in Los Angeles.
I was waiting for the railroad there and got my job waiting for the railroad there. So you stayed out there there? A while.

I stayed out there from 19 from October. I must have got in Los Angeles from 1919 by October the first or second. And it was the funnest thing when I got off the train I had on a straw hat in October. And I guess the people out there was looking at me, you know, well it was hot just like it is this year when I left. And we got off the train I had a straw hat on. I felt so embarrassed and ashamed. That's a warm air chair though. Yes indeed, having a straw hat on. We played at the Cadillac in Los Angeles, I guess Manuel told you that.
Yes, he told us something about the date.
Did you know Jolly Roll Morton there in O'Hanel?
I never did see him. He was in California at that same time. He was there, yeah. I never did see Jolly Roll. I often heard of him about him.

Fess says he would come there and sneak in and play on the piano in the morning there. In the morning, but he never would come back with the band. Never come around to see the band. No, because I didn't know Jolly Roll.
No.
No, I didn't know Jolly Roll.
He was in Los Angeles at that time.
At that very time. What do you know about that? The Spikes Brothers, did you meet them? Spike Brothers, yeah.

Red Spikes, yeah. Johnny Spikes, yeah. Well, we played at the Dreamland for them. You see, after we left the Cadillac, we went down and played for Spikes. Spike Brothers. And they raided that John and police beat Johnny Spikes, so it was terrible. He was a tenor man. Beat himself in terrible. I never forget that. Yeah? Yes, indeed. What were they raided for?
Prohibition then? Yeah, it was Prohibition.

It was Prohibition then. I guess they must have been selling liquor, you know, imagine, so under the cover, you know. We didn't ever know it. I imagine that's what it was about. Yeah. And I know they closed up the joint. He had a place. The Dreamland Cafe was fourth in Stanford. 
in Los Angeles. And I stayed out to Los Angeles until March the 4th, 1921, from 1919 to 1921.
Well, I think, did you ever meet Dink Johnson, a drummer and a piano player?
Yeah, oh yeah, I met Dink. Oh yes, indeed. What become of him?

He died in 1954, I believe, up in Portland at his brother's place. I made some records of him about 15 years ago. What was his brother's name now? I can't remember, it was Bill Johnson, the namesplayer. Bill Johnson, I believe. This is another brother, I can't think of his name now.
Yeah, that's the one I knew, Bill Johnson. They had another brother.

Yeah, and there was another one that played guitar or something. That's right, that's right. But I only met Bill and the Dink. And Dink. Dink died just in 54. Yeah. Was he old? Born in 92, so he was eight years older than you.
Yeah, that's the name. He was about 62 when he died. Yeah, they tell me he's a New Orleans boy from across the lake.

He's sliding out. Yeah, he's all over in there somewhere. Maybe Biloxi, I'm not sure. Bill Ford along in there. Yeah, that's what I heard from over the lake. Uh-huh. He says he told everybody he was born in New Orleans, but he was just near here.

No, over the lake. It wasn't good in here. No, it wasn't here, no, over the lake, because I didn't know him. First time I... Did he ever play with you out there? No, he never did play. We'd seen him play with someone else.
Yeah. I think he played the Black and Pan band. Did you hear them? Yeah, Ernest Johnson. Was that, um, the name of Southern? I can't think of his name. That's right, Harry Southern.

He's a trombone player. That was the leader. That was the trombone player. He was a leader. Ernest Johnson was with them? Yeah, Ernest Johnson. We call him Nene. Bright fella. What did he play? Something. That's Ernest... That's, that's Peele's brother. You heard of Lil' Peele? Yeah, and that's... Well, that's his brother. Nene. Nene, yeah, yeah. Nene Poico. Poico is his real name. That's right, that's right, that's right. Ernest Johnson is Dr. Ernest. But he changed... No, no, he changed his name out there. Yeah. Oh, sure, he changed his name. Changed his name to Johnson. So Poico. Yeah, sure, that was such a funny name, you know. Yeah. Yeah, he's a garra.

He's not there, he is. If I remember rightly, Dink told me that they used to tell him that he was their brother or cousin or something sometimes. Did he? Did he? Yeah. He wasn't related at all, but they'd tell people that. Sometime, you know, I don't know why. Yeah, I guess so.
Well, didn't he play with the superior? That's what Lawrence Morrero told me. Who, Dink?

Ernest Johnson, Ernest Cuoco, Nene. Well, I don't know. That might have been for my time. Yeah, well, that's what he said. He played with him. He played with him. Well, I went out in Los Angeles, I found him out there. Oh, yeah. Yeah, I found him. He had been out there a long time.

He played with that piano player, Sonny Clay, huh, too, out there. Sonny Clay? You know him? No, I don't know. He was a drummer and a piano player. No, Sonny Clay. I guess he came late on that, but Cuoco recorded on Coronet with him. Oh, I see.

Well, I think I just remember the drummer there. Was it Ben Varders, the drummer with the Black and Tan? Did you ever hear him? Who? Varders. Varder. I think it was Ben Varders. What kind of music was out there in the local bands in California? Was it anything like the style of the Marlene's band? No, it wasn't. That's why we taken so. That's what I wondered.
That's why we taken. See, now the Black and Tan band was the best band there, you know, see. Trying to play like us, you know. But after we went there, then.
They didn't really have the style. No, they didn't have it at all. No, they didn't have the style. We wrapped it up when we went there.

Yeah. Yes, indeed. But Buddy P.T. and I believe Charlie Love was out there before us, wasn't he? Did he ever tell you? I believe, no, not Charlie. Frankie Duesen went out. Frankie Duesen? Charlie Love didn't go with him? I don't know. Must have been Buddy P.T. Buddy and Frankie Duesen. Oh, Buddy and Frankie. When I heard that, yeah, I heard they went out there.

And Joe Oliver didn't go out until about 1921. He took his band out. Yeah, I was back here. You were back there. He stayed out there a good while, didn't he? Quite a while in San Francisco and then stopped in Los Angeles a while.
There's a lot of bands in California, a lot of people out there. Yeah, oh, yes. I was out there in October.
Just took a trip, you know. When did you first play in parades? You mentioned with Ridgely. That was your first parade band.

My first parade band? No, I didn't play with Ridgely. My first parade band. I don't believe I can remember what band I played with first. I knew I was a member of the Onward Brass Band, Manuel Perez, you know. That was the Manuel, and you played with him? Yeah, that was the Onward Brass Band. That was the first time you were a regular member of a band? A regular member of a brass band. Onward Brass Band.
How many were in that band about? Ten. Ten. Ten. How many trumpets? Do you remember? Three. Three?

Emanuel Perez, Maurice Duran, and sometimes Ricard. But I can't remember the other regular member. No, but Ricard. I remember who the trombones were. Yank Johnson, and we used a guy called Gaia. You know the guy who used to play banjo? Butler rap. Yeah, butler rap. That's right. He played trombone. I didn't know that. Yeah, he played trombone in our brass band a long time.

They had alto horns or saxes or anything? Yeah, we had real alto. Old man Bob Rand. Oh yes. He played, and who baritone played? Tats Daddy. Oh yes, Alexander. Yeah, old man Alexander. Adolph, his name is Adolph.
Adolph Adolph Adolph, that's right. That's who played baritone with us. Who was this? And we had clarinet Joe Watson. You heard of Joe Watson clarinet player? We had him.
Did you play snare or bass drum? Snare. Snare. Snare. Henry Martin played bass drum.
Henry Martin. Black Benny played first, until he got killed, and Henry Martin played until the band broke up.

How was Manuel Perez? Some people talk like he was the greatest of ever, and others say that he wasn't such a hot trumpet player, just a note reader, and that he really couldn't think anything. How did you like him? What did he sound like? He was a legitimate trumpet player.

Much more legitimate. Yeah, yeah. He wasn't a hot trumpet player, not a jazz trumpet player like of today. That's right, strictly music. That's right, a legitimate trumpet player. Did he have a big tone or? Nice tone, kind of nice tone. But it wasn't a fine tone, you know. It was more of a brass band tone, you see. Yeah. Kind of rough, you know. Loud, high notes. Notes didn't come too high, you see. Fine musician. Yeah, that's what I've heard. Yeah, I worked with him on the Roof Garden, Maurice Durand and I, and Buddy Johnson, he was a Yanks brother. We worked on the Roof Garden two years from 25 to 27. We had Emmanuel Perez, Buddy Johnson, myself, Eddie Sherry, you heard of him. And Lil' Caffrey, Darius Boyd on the guitar. You heard of Caffrey, Darius Boyd, and him. And, uh...
Who was the alto player? Was it before Tad's or after him?
We had Sherry and Tad. You had them both, huh? We had Sherry and Tad. And, uh, piano player, what's her name? Still on Josephine Street. She played with Celestine Lakeley. Uh...
Uh... Ken Ed? Ken Ed? Mercedee's... That's it. Mercedee's. She worked up there with us two years.

Mercedee's going on the three years. Then after, yeah, that's right. Then after she worked with us, uh... I see old Blanchett. You heard of him. Oh, yes. And he worked with us. What's he doing? I see. He's a school teacher. And we had a teacher at 35. Teacher at 35.
Yeah, very awesome. 35, Rampart and Girard. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

Then we had, uh, Dandy Lewis on bass. You heard of him. Yeah, I've heard Bess talk about him. That's right. Dandy Lewis. That's who we had on bass. Then after Buddy Johnson left, we taken Earl Umphrey on trombone. He played up there with us. Then... Manny Mineta come up there with us a while. Yeah, he told us he did. Yeah, he come up. He played with us a while. We had a nice band. Five band. We used to have two bands. Celestine, our band, and they had the big carnival bars. They hired two bands. Sometime they'd hire Faith Marable. He had his band up there. He had his whole band up there. Oh, yeah. Come off the boat. Come up there and play late. You know what I see? Oh, yeah. He had a fine band. 25, from 25 to 27. Fine band. Who was with Faith about that time? Around by that time, he had Dewey Jackson. You remember Dewey? Well, I never met him. Fine trumpet, yeah. Fine trumpet playing. We had, uh, had this boy on trombone. Little Light Boy out of St. Louis. He had a band of his own after that. Harvey Lightfoot. Harvey Lightfoot.
Something like that? Or was it Lawson?

No, Harvey Lightfoot. Harvey Lightfoot. Yeah, that's his name. He's on record, too. Yeah. Harvey, wait. Is he still living? I don't know. Harvey Lightfoot. Mm-hmm. And he had a drummer. What's his drummer name? He live in Chicago. Now, a singing drummer. He sings well. Camel. Oh, yes. Camel. Floyd. That's right. Floyd Camel. That's right. He on piano. And, uh, what's this trombone player name? Natty Dominic? Nat, Nat, Nat, Nat. Nat, Nat. A trombone. Fine trombone. That's him. That's right. That story. St. Louis. That's right. That story. That's him. Fine trombone player. Yeah, let me see now. Who else on? Well, sometime he had old man Kimball on bass. Kimball's father. Yeah. Yeah, he and him. He worked for him a long time. I believe he was on bass then. I've waited for him a long time. And he had another little guy on banjo. He told me he went to penitentiary. He killed a man in New York. A little light fella. I can't think of his name. He must have went penitentiary. My older. Early thirties. Yeah. Fine banjo player. A little light boy. If I had to call his name, you might know him. Fine. Gets fine. Open the door. Looks like we have company.
I think before Andy came in, you were telling about when you played up the roof garden and Fates band.
Did they have two bands that were lights? Two bands. Two bands. Yeah. They had a better band. A fine band.
It was always a big band, but I bet your band played just as exciting as they did. I guess we imagined it. Yeah, sure. Just because they were bigger, it was better.
We thought they were bigger. But they were fine. Yeah.
What about Sam Morgan? I want to get on that.
Sam? Sam? Yeah. Well, Sam, I played with Sam Morgan from 1921 until 25.
Did he have any good men and his man? Well, yeah. We had me. I was a fan. That's what you stopped. I was a fan. I was a fan.
Ed Yank Johnson. Sam Morgan.
Joe Watson. Ed Get It Taps and Daniel. We went on guitar.
Buddy Manaday.
Remember that Sonny? Sonny? No, no. No, he used to be a comedian.
Buddy Manaday is right.
Buddy Manaday. That's before he went with Buddy Petit, huh?
Yeah. Buddy Manaday and Lil T-Boy on the bass. A fella that called T-Boy. Eddie Gilmore?
Yeah, that's right. That was our original band.

Then after Eddie Gilmore got out, we had taken Simon, Simon Moreira. He played with us a long time. Then after Buddy Manaday got out, we had taken Guy A.C. Butler Rapp and he stayed with us about three years and I left in 25 and that's when I went to the roof garden from 25 to 26 and I left and I left from 25 to 27, Manuel Perez. And after I left Manuel Perez, I went down to the La Vida.
That's the taxi dance hall.

The street taxi dance hall. Our band consists of Raymond Brown, which is Clifford. We call him Clifford, but his name is Raymond. He lives in Frisco. Bat Brown's nephew. Yeah, yeah. And him, and Handley, Williams Kelly, Lewis Gibbons, and Sidney Flutcher. That was our band at the La Vida. How long did you stay there about? I stayed there. I went there in 27. I stayed there about a year.
What hours did you have?
Oh, hours. Hours. Hours. That's all it was. That's all? That's all it was. Hours. Hours. Let's talk about that.
Did you take a turn about getting off the stand to get a little rest sometime, or how'd you do that?
Yeah, well, I just walk off the stand, and somebody else would get on the drum, you know, until I come back. We'd take time.
Any of the other guys in the band play drums?

Yeah, Raymond Brown. He would play. Then Handley, he would get on the drum, you know. Play a waltz, you know, until I come back. Yeah. Then after I left there in 29, around 20, yeah, I don't know, around 27, I played there about a year, 28. Celestine and Ridgely's band broke up then. That's when the band split. Well, I went with Ridgely. See, Ridgely made up a band. See, I went with Ridgely, paid with Ridgely down at Pete Hoyman's place. What do you call it? Planetation? Yeah. Planetation. That's right. I worked there, we worked there for about a year, and then we just jobbed around, you know, just gigged around. Yeah. That band consists of me, Ridgely, Emma Barry. Tip된 stuff there.
Shots, Handy, Sales. What did Handy play in those days? Alto and clarinet. Did he play much clarinet then? Oh, lots of clarinet. I can't think of this one. I'm a mic now.
About sales, how did he rate among the guitar players and banjo players?
He used to put on all these hats, changed hats all the time. He had about ten or twelve hats at night. Not played that many bass for that. I was playing with them.
You don't have to be afraid to talk, I don't know, you're out there and there.

Yeah, he was. Jimmy Jones? Jimmy Jones. Jimmy. Jimmy. Jimmy. You forgot? Yeah, Jimmy. You know what I was trying to think was playing with us at Pete Ornans, played bass, but we might not have a bass then.
How did Sales rate in those days? He was a nice, fine guitar player. I just wondered who would be among the best guitar players in town. Oh yeah, he was fine, yes indeed.

He always was a musician, you see. He learned the right way. Oh yeah, a musician. That's what I did. He was great, good. Always have been. What about P-Rom's band? P-Rom's band? I played with P-Rom's band from 32 to 35. I played with P-Rom's band. I played with P-Rom's band. I played with P-Rom's band. I played with with Song that was after that. He broke up the band. Now his band consists of P. Ron's band, when I first started playing, consists of me, P. Ron, Lil' Allegrette Alexander, Eddie Pearson on trombone, Joe Phillips, Leo Dejon, Sales, Arthur Durden, Ellia Taylor, and Simon Moreira on the page. That's the band on the book. That's the band on the book. And Harry Wells was our singer. He died. He lived too fast. Fine singer.

segments.chapter: Opening talk: pianists and Buddy Petit
segments.title: Records made in California c.1921 and Fred Washington
segments.summary: The interviewer says he made records in California around 1921 with Fred Washington; Williams recalls Washington playing at a nightclub in a makeshift band.

segments.chapter: Opening talk: pianists and Buddy Petit
segments.title: Piano players around New Orleans and Buddy Christian
segments.summary: Williams names pianists he knew or knew of, including Steve Lewis, Tony Jackson, Udell Wilson, Arthur Campbell and Buddy Christian.

segments.chapter: Opening talk: pianists and Buddy Petit
segments.title: Working with Buddy Petit in 1921, his band and ragtime
segments.summary: Williams played about eight months with Buddy Petit after returning from Los Angeles, before joining Sam Morgan; he lists Petit's men and says ragtime became jazz with the same beat.

segments.title: El Paso 1936-51: Bob Watts and a mixed Mexican band
segments.summary: Williams was in El Paso from 1936 to 1951; he led a mixed band with trumpeter Bob Watts and Mexican musicians who played American music but not New Orleans style, though he taught them tunes.

segments.title: Learning Mexican music as a non-reading drummer and band manager
segments.summary: Playing the Southwest meant Mexican, hillbilly and jazz; Williams, who could not read, picked up Mexican music by ear and impressed the local musicians.

segments.chapter: Ridgley, La Vida, Piron and the Minstrels
segments.title: Career sequence after Perez: Ridgley, La Vida, Piron
segments.summary: Williams recounts going from Perez to La Vida, Ridgley's band, back to La Vida, then Piron from 1932 to 1935.

segments.chapter: Ridgley, La Vida, Piron and the Minstrels
segments.title: Riverboat trip with Piron on the J.S. in 1934
segments.summary: The Piron band made a tramp-steamer trip up the Ohio and Mississippi as far as Red Wing, Minnesota.

segments.chapter: Ridgley, La Vida, Piron and the Minstrels
segments.title: Piron's band personnel and breakup, 1932-35
segments.summary: Williams explains Piron's band broke up and was remade, and lists its members and singer Harold Wells.

segments.chapter: Ridgley, La Vida, Piron and the Minstrels
segments.title: Leaving with the Georgia Minstrels and being stranded in El Paso
segments.summary: After a stint back at La Vida, Williams left in February 1936 with the Georgia Minstrels, was stranded in El Paso, and stayed; he knew only Kimberl Dial in the show band.

segments.chapter: Ridgley, La Vida, Piron and the Minstrels
segments.title: La Vida band personnel
segments.summary: Williams names the La Vida players, including Ernest Kelly, Lewis Gibbons, Handley, Raymond Brown and Sidney Flewger.

segments.title: Sam Morgan's band, the slapstick and personnel changes
segments.summary: Williams was with Sam Morgan 1921-25, says the slapstick originated with another player, calls the band tops, and discusses the changes of personnel.

segments.title: Interview opening: name, date and address
segments.summary: The interviewers establish Williams's name, the date, his home address, and who is present.

segments.title: Birth in New Orleans and family without musicians
segments.summary: Williams was born September 1, 1900, in the Third Ward; he was an only child and no one in his family played music.

segments.title: First music heard: parades, brass bands and drummer Henry Martin
segments.summary: As a child Williams followed the Monday parades and the Onward, Excelsior and Ridgley's Tuxedo bands, and admired left-handed drummer Henry Martin.

segments.title: First job with the Columbia Band at Butcher Hill, age 16
segments.summary: At sixteen Williams played his first job with the Columbia Band, naming its members including Tick Chambers, Ernest Kelly and Roy Palmer.

segments.title: Learning drums: pots and pans, renting a drum, no lessons
segments.summary: Williams began on his mother's pots at about eight, rented a drum from Dave Puykins, never took lessons and played left-handed.

segments.title: Joining Kid Ory in Henry Martin's place at the Palm Garden
segments.summary: Williams subbed for Henry Martin and played with Ory at the Palm Garden, with Mutt Carey, Johnny Dodds and others.

segments.title: Before Los Angeles: Buddy Petit and what became of Wade Whaley
segments.summary: Williams was with Buddy Petit before leaving for Los Angeles in 1919, and discusses the group that went out and Wade Whaley's whereabouts.

segments.title: Other early drummers: Henry Zeno, Ernest Rapania, Baby Dodds
segments.summary: Williams comments on drummers of the teens, including Henry Zeno, Ernest Rapania and Baby Dodds.

segments.title: Playing at Pete Lala's with Ory, King Oliver and Louis Armstrong, 1917
segments.summary: After the Columbia Band, Williams sat in for Oliver's drummer at Ory's weekend job at Pete Lala's, with Armstrong also sitting in, just before Storyville closed.

segments.title: Red Happy, Ernest Rogers and the young players
segments.summary: The interviewers ask about Red Happy and Ernest Rogers, and Williams says Rogers never played with the outstanding bands.

segments.title: Going to Los Angeles in 1919 with Ory's group
segments.summary: Williams went west with Ory's men, stayed on after the band broke up, and recalls arriving in October in a straw hat; they played the Cadillac.

segments.title: Jelly Roll Morton in California
segments.summary: Williams never saw or knew Jelly Roll Morton, though he was in California at the same time.

segments.title: The Spikes Brothers and the Dreamland raid
segments.summary: Williams's band played for the Spikes Brothers at the Dreamland after the Cadillac; a Prohibition raid ended it, and he stayed in Los Angeles until March 1921.

segments.title: Dink Johnson and Ernest Johnson (Nene) in Los Angeles
segments.summary: Discussion of Dink Johnson and the drummer Ernest Johnson, who Williams says changed his name out West, and what they played.

segments.title: California bands compared with New Orleans style
segments.summary: Williams says the Los Angeles Black and Tan band tried to play like New Orleans bands, and recalls who went west before and after him.

segments.title: Onward Brass Band lineup with Manuel Perez
segments.summary: Williams recalls his first regular brass-band job, with the Onward Brass Band, and lists its trumpets, trombones, altos, clarinet and drummers.

segments.title: Manuel Perez's playing and the Roof Garden band, 1925-27
segments.summary: Williams describes Perez as a legitimate brass-band trumpeter and lists the Roof Garden band he worked in from 1925 to 1927.

segments.title: Roof Garden rivals: Faith Marable's band and Harvey Lightfoot
segments.summary: The Roof Garden hired two bands; Williams recalls Faith Marable's visiting riverboat band and its players, then a break when company arrives.

segments.chapter: Sam Morgan, La Vida and Ridgley
segments.title: Sam Morgan's original band and later changes
segments.summary: Williams lists the original Sam Morgan band, 1921-25, and who replaced departing members before he left for the Roof Garden.

segments.chapter: Sam Morgan, La Vida and Ridgley
segments.title: The La Vida taxi dance hall band and its long hours
segments.summary: Williams went to La Vida in 1927 and lists the band; he describes the long hours and taking breaks while others drummed.

segments.chapter: Sam Morgan, La Vida and Ridgley
segments.title: Ridgley's band at the Plantation: personnel and guitarist Sales
segments.summary: After Celestin and Ridgley split, Williams joined Ridgley's band at the Plantation; talk of its players, Handy, and guitarist Sales.

segments.chapter: Sam Morgan, La Vida and Ridgley
segments.title: Piron's band from 1932 to 1935 and its singer
segments.summary: Williams repeats that he was with Piron from 1932 to 1935 and lists the band, with singer Harold Wells.
